tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

1	# User-visible audit trail
2	
3	* **Author:** Alexis Cramatte
4	* **Date:** 2026-11-03
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	ZaimuTomo gets a read-only page where the user can see what changed in their
9	data, when it changed, and who changed it: the user, or a named system process
10	such as document processing, startup recovery, or a maintenance task. The page
11	is for looking only. It has no undo and no retry. Later, an MCP endpoint could
12	expose the same log to agents.
13	
14	The app already writes an audit table, `event_logs`, but it is narrow:
15	
16	- It covers four review and posting events.
17	- Two of those four are written after the change commits, on a best-effort
18	  basis. If the insert fails, the row is lost and only a warning is logged:
19	  `Review.reject_invoice` (`lib/zaimu_tomo/review.ex:96`) and
20	  `Accounting.post_entry` (`lib/zaimu_tomo/accounting.ex:352`).
21	- Its `invoice_id` column holds an extraction id for review events and a
22	  journal-entry id for posting events, with nothing in the row to say which.
23	- No page shows it.
24	
25	This feature turns that table into a complete, user-readable history.
26	
27	## Analysis
28	
29	Six independent reviewers looked at the hypothesis. Their findings, merged and
30	sorted by theme:
31	
32	### 1. Completeness is the main risk, not storage or UI
33	
34	A history log that misses changes is worse than none, because the user will
35	trust its gaps. The reviewers listed every write path for the covered data. These
36	are the ones a simple "log it in the context function" approach would miss:
37	
38	- **Database cascades.** Deleting a document cascades through
39	  `extracted_content` to `review_decisions`. Deleting a financial account
40	  cascades to `balance_snapshots`. No Elixir code sees those child deletes.
41	- **`Repo.update_all` in `FingerprintBackfill`** (`fingerprint_backfill.ex:128`).
42	  It writes documents without going through a changeset and doesn't return the
43	  rows. The same task also changes journal entries (sets the reuse
44	  confirmation) and keeps `updated_at` unchanged on purpose.
45	- **Public writers that nothing in the app calls yet.** Any future caller would
46	  skip the audit:
47	  - `Accounting.create_from_decision/2`, which only tests use
48	  - `Review.update_review_decision/2`
49	  - `FinancialAccounts.update_financial_account/3` and `delete_financial_account/2`
50	- **Data migrations** that run raw `UPDATE` statements, for example
51	  `20260804100341_set_base_currency_default.exs`.
52	- **Dev seeds.** They would appear as user actions unless they get their own actor.
53	
54	No web or mix-task code calls `Repo` directly, so writing events from the
55	contexts reaches everything except the cascades, `update_all`, and migrations.
56	Those need explicit handling (see Key Decisions).
57	
58	### 2. Every audited write must commit together with its change
59	
60	Decision D10 in `docs/architecture.md` already requires this for approve and
61	amend. Rejection and posting do not follow it, and none of the new paths
62	(documents, accounts, balances, settings) have any audit write yet. The
63	reviewers agree the rule should extend to every audited change: if the audit
64	insert fails, the change rolls back. The case against: a bug in the audit
65	insert would block a save. For a permanent single-user ledger, a loud failure
66	is better than a silent gap, and tests can catch audit-insert bugs.
67	
68	### 3. "Before/after values" conflicts with "no document text"
69	
70	The issuer, invoice number, amount, date and `reason_for_payment` on review
71	decisions and journal entries are all LLM output from reading the document.
72	Read literally, "never store document text" forbids the diffs the page exists
73	to show. Existing `invoice_amended` rows already store the full
74	`amended_data`. Other fields must never appear at all:
75	
76	- fingerprints (`content_sha256`, `source_document_sha256`). Architecture §8
77	  says they are "never rendered", and the schemas mark them `redact: true`.
78	- `hashed_password`
79	- `raw_llm_response`, `analysis` and `error_details`
80	
81	The reviewers recommend:
82	
83	- **An allowlist of fields per entity, not a denylist.** With a denylist, every
84	  new column would leak into the log until someone excluded it.
85	- **Ecto's redacted fields** (`__schema__(:redact_fields)`) stripped as a
86	  backstop.
87	- **A clear boundary**, which the author has since set more strictly than the
88	  reviewers proposed (decision 2 below): extracted invoice fields are not
89	  recorded at all, only user-entered fields are.
90	
91	### 4. Most of the coverage list already has history
92	
93	Some covered items already keep their own history:
94	
95	- Extraction attempts are separate `extracted_content` rows, never edited.
96	- Balance snapshots are only ever inserted.
97	- Review decisions move forward once.
98	
99	Only about eight call sites overwrite or delete user data:
100	
101	- `post_entry` (re-categorizing, tax claim)
102	- account update and delete
103	- document update and delete
104	- profile update
105	- reject
106	- the fingerprint backfill
107	
108	Logging the insert-only data again duplicates facts. The other option is to
109	build the page as a read model, like `ZaimuTomo.Activity`, that merges
110	`event_logs` with those existing rows. The zoom-out reviewer prefers that.
111	Others prefer one table for one consistent "who" column and simpler paging.
112	The author chose one table (decision 4 below).
113	
114	### 5. "Who" needs an owner, an actor, and a way to carry it
115	
116	- **Two fields, not one.** A single `user_id` cannot hold both whose data it is
117	  and who did it.
118	- **Actors are lost across Oban.** Upload, user retry, Recovery, and a Lifeline
119	  rescue all end in the same `Worker` write. The job args carry no origin, so
120	  these four cases cannot be told apart.
121	- **Module names change.** Entries are kept forever, so the actor needs a
122	  stable key such as `system.ocr_job` or `release.fingerprint_backfill`, with a
123	  display label.
124	- **The actor has no carrier.** `Scope` holds only `user`. Review and
125	  Accounting take a bare `user_id`. Release tasks have neither.
126	
127	### 6. Entries must outlive the records they describe
128	
129	Documents and accounts can be hard-deleted. A foreign key from an audit row to
130	its subject would either block the delete or delete the history with it. Each
131	entry needs:
132	
133	- a typed subject (`subject_type` + `subject_id`) with no foreign key
134	- a short label captured at write time, for example a filename, or issuer and
135	  date
136	- a format version, so later field renames don't break old entries
137	
138	### 7. The page sits next to an existing "Activity" page
139	
140	`/activity` and the dashboard's recent-activity widget already show
141	chronological feeds. Activity shows where each document stands now; the new
142	page shows what changed. The naming and placement must keep the two apart.
143	
144	The page also needs:
145	
146	- human labels instead of raw field names
147	- formatted money and dates
148	- names in place of ids where possible
149	- links to records that still exist
150	- filters for actor, entity type and a single record
151	- keyset pagination
152	- a way to collapse bulk system runs, for example "backfill updated 214
153	  documents"
154	
155	### 8. Rollout and existing data
156	
157	- **Deploy order.** Migrations run *after* the new container is live
158	  (`docs/deployment.md:99`). If the new code writes columns the migration has
159	  not added yet, every approve and amend fails until `kamal migrate` runs.
160	  - The change must ship in two releases: first create `audit_events`, then
161	    start writing to it. See Staging below.
162	- **No legacy rows.** `audit_events` starts empty on the day it ships.
163	  Nothing is copied from `event_logs`, so the page shows no history from
164	  before the release.
165	- **Timestamps** have one-second precision, so events from one transaction tie.
166	  Fix: `utc_datetime_usec`, order by `(inserted_at, id)`, and index
167	  `(user_id, inserted_at DESC, id DESC)`.
168	- **Tests that query `EventLog`** by `invoice_id` or `metadata` keys need
169	  updating: `accounting_test.exs`, `review_test.exs`.
170	
171	### 9. Cost is not a concern
172	
173	One user generates tens of audited changes a day: about 10k–30k rows a year,
174	a few MB with allowlisted diffs. Keeping entries forever costs almost nothing.
175	No pruning is needed.
176	
177	## Goals vs. Non-Goals
178	
179	* **In-Scope Goals:**
180	  * A read-only, newest-first audit page inside the existing
181	    `live_session :require_authenticated_user`. Reads filter by `%Scope{}`.
182	  * Every audited change writes its audit entry in the same transaction,
183	    including the two paths that are best-effort today.
184	  * Coverage:
185	    * changes to documents, review decisions, journal entries, postings,
186	      tax claims, financial accounts and balance snapshots, and the profile
187	      settings (display name, base currency)
188	    * one event per final extraction outcome, with the error class only
189	    * system and maintenance actions, each with a named actor
190	  * Field diffs limited to an allowlist per entity. Sensitive changes are
191	    recorded as "changed" with no value.
192	  * Entries readable after their subject is deleted.
193	  * Append-only, guarded against app bugs.
194	  * A serializable read function (`Audit.list_entries(scope, filters, cursor)`)
195	    that a later MCP endpoint can reuse.
196	  * Docs updated: `docs/architecture.md` §4, §5, §6.1, §8 (data model,
197	    security, tests), §9 (new decision), §10, §11, §12; `docs/operations.md`
198	    for any backfill or rollback steps.
199	* **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:**
200	  * Undo, retry, or any other action from the page.
201	  * The MCP endpoint and the authentication it would need.
202	  * Diagnostic detail: OCR text, LLM payloads, TypeSafe shadow results,
203	    per-attempt retry noise.
204	  * Deploy-time environment config.
205	  * Login and session tokens (unless decided otherwise).
206	  * Guarding against the operator. Append-only protects against app bugs, not
207	    someone with `psql`.
208	  * Retention, pruning, archiving.
209	
210	## Alternatives Weighed
211	
212	* **Carbonite (Postgres triggers with a transaction-metadata row).** It catches
213	  cascades, `update_all` and raw SQL, and is transactional by construction.
214	  Rejected as the default by the reviewers:
215	  * It records row changes, not domain events, so every table needs a
216	    translation layer before entries read like "Approved invoice X".
217	  * Every write path still has to insert a Carbonite transaction row first.
218	    That is the same wrapping work as explicit events.
219	  * It captures noise (`updated_at`-only changes, shadow writes) that has to be
220	    filtered out.
221	  * It captures every column by default, which works against the allowlist.
222	  * It remains the fallback if explicit events prove to leak.
223	* **ExAudit (Repo wrapper, actor in the process dictionary).** Rejected:
224	  * It doesn't see `update_all`, `insert_all`, `delete_all` or cascades.
225	  * Process-dictionary actors must be set again in every LiveView and Oban
226	    process.
227	  * It records row diffs, not domain events.
228	* **PaperTrail-style versioning.** Rejected. It gives the same guarantees as
229	  explicit events, plus a dependency and full-row snapshots by default.
230	* **A hand-written generic trigger (`to_jsonb(OLD)`/`to_jsonb(NEW)`).**
231	  Rejected. It captures every column, including fingerprints, account numbers
232	  and LLM payloads.
233	* **Explicit events plus a trigger-based catch-all table to check
234	  completeness.** Rejected as too heavy for a single-user app. It means two
235	  sources of truth.
236	* **Hash-chained, tamper-evident log.** Rejected. The operator could rebuild
237	  the chain, so it adds no real protection here.
238	* **Merged read model** (the page merges `audit_events` with existing
239	  `balance_snapshots` and `extracted_content` rows, like `Activity` does).
240	  Rejected by author: the existing rows have no actor column, so they can't
241	  say who made the change. Paging across several sources is awkward. One
242	  table costs only a few KB of duplicated data.
243	* **A Postgres view** (`UNION ALL` over the same tables). Rejected by author:
244	  it is the merged read model written in SQL. The source tables still have no
245	  actor, and every branch of the union needs its own index for keyset paging.
246	  A view could still be added later as a read layer over `audit_events`
247	  alone, for example for the MCP endpoint.
248	* **Reusing `event_logs`.** Rejected by author. Its `invoice_id` column holds
249	  ids from two different tables, its `status` column means nothing for an
250	  audit entry, and it has no actor. A new table avoids carrying those over.
251	  `event_logs` is frozen once `audit_events` covers the same events.
252	* **Nulling out the user on deletion (`on_delete: :nilify_all`).** Rejected:
253	  it works by updating audit rows, which the append-only trigger forbids.
254	
255	## Key Decisions & Staging for Next Steps
256	
257	**Converging recommendation from the reviewers.** All six agree on:
258	
259	- explicit `Audit.record(...)` calls from each context, inside the same
260	  `Ecto.Multi` as the change
261	- one shared audit module, replacing the private `write_event_log` copies in
262	  `review.ex` and `accounting.ex`
263	- an actor passed explicitly, not through process state (decision 6 below
264	  carries it on `%Scope{}`)
265	- allowlisted field diffs in a `changes` jsonb column, with event context such
266	  as a rejection reason kept separate
267	- typed subjects with no foreign key, plus a label captured at write time
268	- `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` and `BEFORE TRUNCATE` triggers on the audit table
269	- coverage enforced by a test per public mutating function, and optionally a
270	  Credo check that flags `Repo.*` writes outside the audit helper
271	
272	**Decided by the author (2026-11-04):**
273	
274	1. **What one entry is.** One domain event per user or system operation.
275	   Each event holds a list of field diffs for the rows that operation changed.
276	2. **No extracted invoice fields in the trail.** Fields the LLM read from the
277	   document never appear in the log, as values or as diffs. These include
278	   issuer, invoice number, amount, date, currency and `reason_for_payment`,
279	   and the journal entry `description` copied from it. An amendment is
280	   recorded as an event that names the changed fields ("issuer, amount
281	   changed") with no values. User-entered fields can be diffed: category,
282	   need/want, notes, rejection reason, account names, balances and profile
283	   settings.
284	3. **New `audit_events` table. `event_logs` is frozen in a later release.** Its
285	   writers keep working until `audit_events` covers the same events, then they
286	   are removed. The table and its rows stay in place, unread, and none of its
287	   rows are copied. The author
288	   recalled `event_logs` as a possible event-sourcing experiment, but the
289	   written record says otherwise: spec `002-review-ocr-data`, the commit that
290	   added it (`1659de5`) and the `Review` moduledoc all describe it as the
291	   review audit trail, and no spec, doc or commit message mentions event
292	   sourcing. Session history does not reach back to when it was added. The
293	   docs must say that `audit_events` is the audit trail and that `event_logs`
294	   is a frozen, older review-only log (architecture §4, §5, §8 data model, and
295	   a new §9 decision that supersedes the audit part of D10).
296	4. **One table.** Every audited operation writes an `audit_events` row,
297	   including actions whose data already lives in insert-only tables (balance
298	   snapshots, extraction outcomes).
299	5. **Cascaded deletes and bulk updates are recorded explicitly.** A parent
300	   delete event lists what was deleted with it ("2 extractions, 1 review
301	   decision"; "5 balance snapshots"). `FingerprintBackfill` is rewritten to
302	   return the updated rows with their `user_id`. It then writes one summary
303	   event per run and one "fingerprint added" event per document, with no
304	   values. No database triggers capture changes.
305	6. **Actor carried on `%Scope{}`.** `Scope` gains an actor, for example
306	   `Scope.system(:recovery)` or `Scope.system(:fingerprint_backfill)`, and the
307	   writing functions in `Review` and `Accounting` move from a bare `user_id`
308	   to a `Scope`. OCR job args gain `initiated_by: upload | user_retry |
309	   recovery`, so the worker can rebuild the actor.
310	8. **Page name: "Audit log".** It is a separate page from Activity, inside
311	   `live_session :require_authenticated_user`.
312	9. **Success criteria (testable):**
313	   - every covered write path produces exactly one audit event, in the same
314	     transaction as the change
315	   - a test proves that no redacted field, extracted invoice field, or
316	     forbidden field reaches `audit_events`
317	   - a test with two users proves one user's events never appear for the other
318	
319	7. **Deleting a user keeps their events.** `audit_events.user_id` (the owner)
320	   and the actor's user id are plain integer columns with no foreign key, so
321	   deleting a user neither fails nor touches audit rows. When the page or a
322	   later reader shows an actor whose user no longer exists, it shows a
323	   placeholder ("Deleted user"). Initials were rejected because they would
324	   have to be stored in each event, keeping part of the name after deletion.
325	   Record this in architecture §11. The frozen `event_logs.user_id` foreign
326	   key (`on_delete: :nothing`) still blocks deleting a user with old rows, so
327	   any future "delete user" feature needs a migration to drop that key.
328	
329	**Staging:**
330	
331	1. A refactor commit first: `Review` and `Accounting` writers take a `Scope`
332	   instead of `user_id`, and `Scope` gains an actor. No behaviour change.
333	2. Release N: create `audit_events` (append-only triggers, index on
334	   `(user_id, inserted_at DESC, id DESC)`). Because the table is new, the
335	   triggers can ship with it, and the previous release never touches it.
336	3. Release N+1: the shared `Audit` module and all writers. This release also
337	   adds `initiated_by` to the OCR job args and rewrites `FingerprintBackfill`.
338	   Old jobs without `initiated_by` default to `upload`.
339	4. Release N+1 or N+2: the "Audit log" page and its read function
340	   `Audit.list_entries(scope, filters, cursor)`.
341	5. Final release, once `audit_events` is confirmed to cover approve, amend,
342	   reject, post and file-reuse events: freeze `event_logs`. Remove its writers
343	   and the `EventLog` schema, and update the tests that query it
344	   (`accounting_test.exs`, `review_test.exs`). Leave the table and its rows in
345	   place.

# User-visible audit trail

* **Author:** Alexis Cramatte
* **Date:** 2026-11-03

## Overview

ZaimuTomo gets a read-only page where the user can see what changed in their
data, when it changed, and who changed it: the user, or a named system process
such as document processing, startup recovery, or a maintenance task. The page
is for looking only. It has no undo and no retry. Later, an MCP endpoint could
expose the same log to agents.

The app already writes an audit table, `event_logs`, but it is narrow:

- It covers four review and posting events.
- Two of those four are written after the change commits, on a best-effort
  basis. If the insert fails, the row is lost and only a warning is logged:
  `Review.reject_invoice` (`lib/zaimu_tomo/review.ex:96`) and
  `Accounting.post_entry` (`lib/zaimu_tomo/accounting.ex:352`).
- Its `invoice_id` column holds an extraction id for review events and a
  journal-entry id for posting events, with nothing in the row to say which.
- No page shows it.

This feature turns that table into a complete, user-readable history.

## Analysis

Six independent reviewers looked at the hypothesis. Their findings, merged and
sorted by theme:

### 1. Completeness is the main risk, not storage or UI

A history log that misses changes is worse than none, because the user will
trust its gaps. The reviewers listed every write path for the covered data. These
are the ones a simple "log it in the context function" approach would miss:

- **Database cascades.** Deleting a document cascades through
  `extracted_content` to `review_decisions`. Deleting a financial account
  cascades to `balance_snapshots`. No Elixir code sees those child deletes.
- **`Repo.update_all` in `FingerprintBackfill`** (`fingerprint_backfill.ex:128`).
  It writes documents without going through a changeset and doesn't return the
  rows. The same task also changes journal entries (sets the reuse
  confirmation) and keeps `updated_at` unchanged on purpose.
- **Public writers that nothing in the app calls yet.** Any future caller would
  skip the audit:
  - `Accounting.create_from_decision/2`, which only tests use
  - `Review.update_review_decision/2`
  - `FinancialAccounts.update_financial_account/3` and `delete_financial_account/2`
- **Data migrations** that run raw `UPDATE` statements, for example
  `20260804100341_set_base_currency_default.exs`.
- **Dev seeds.** They would appear as user actions unless they get their own actor.

No web or mix-task code calls `Repo` directly, so writing events from the
contexts reaches everything except the cascades, `update_all`, and migrations.
Those need explicit handling (see Key Decisions).

### 2. Every audited write must commit together with its change

Decision D10 in `docs/architecture.md` already requires this for approve and
amend. Rejection and posting do not follow it, and none of the new paths
(documents, accounts, balances, settings) have any audit write yet. The
reviewers agree the rule should extend to every audited change: if the audit
insert fails, the change rolls back. The case against: a bug in the audit
insert would block a save. For a permanent single-user ledger, a loud failure
is better than a silent gap, and tests can catch audit-insert bugs.

### 3. "Before/after values" conflicts with "no document text"

The issuer, invoice number, amount, date and `reason_for_payment` on review
decisions and journal entries are all LLM output from reading the document.
Read literally, "never store document text" forbids the diffs the page exists
to show. Existing `invoice_amended` rows already store the full
`amended_data`. Other fields must never appear at all:

- fingerprints (`content_sha256`, `source_document_sha256`). Architecture §8
  says they are "never rendered", and the schemas mark them `redact: true`.
- `hashed_password`
- `raw_llm_response`, `analysis` and `error_details`

The reviewers recommend:

- **An allowlist of fields per entity, not a denylist.** With a denylist, every
  new column would leak into the log until someone excluded it.
- **Ecto's redacted fields** (`__schema__(:redact_fields)`) stripped as a
  backstop.
- **A clear boundary**, which the author has since set more strictly than the
  reviewers proposed (decision 2 below): extracted invoice fields are not
  recorded at all, only user-entered fields are.

### 4. Most of the coverage list already has history

Some covered items already keep their own history:

- Extraction attempts are separate `extracted_content` rows, never edited.
- Balance snapshots are only ever inserted.
- Review decisions move forward once.

Only about eight call sites overwrite or delete user data:

- `post_entry` (re-categorizing, tax claim)
- account update and delete
- document update and delete
- profile update
- reject
- the fingerprint backfill

Logging the insert-only data again duplicates facts. The other option is to
build the page as a read model, like `ZaimuTomo.Activity`, that merges
`event_logs` with those existing rows. The zoom-out reviewer prefers that.
Others prefer one table for one consistent "who" column and simpler paging.
The author chose one table (decision 4 below).

### 5. "Who" needs an owner, an actor, and a way to carry it

- **Two fields, not one.** A single `user_id` cannot hold both whose data it is
  and who did it.
- **Actors are lost across Oban.** Upload, user retry, Recovery, and a Lifeline
  rescue all end in the same `Worker` write. The job args carry no origin, so
  these four cases cannot be told apart.
- **Module names change.** Entries are kept forever, so the actor needs a
  stable key such as `system.ocr_job` or `release.fingerprint_backfill`, with a
  display label.
- **The actor has no carrier.** `Scope` holds only `user`. Review and
  Accounting take a bare `user_id`. Release tasks have neither.

### 6. Entries must outlive the records they describe

Documents and accounts can be hard-deleted. A foreign key from an audit row to
its subject would either block the delete or delete the history with it. Each
entry needs:

- a typed subject (`subject_type` + `subject_id`) with no foreign key
- a short label captured at write time, for example a filename, or issuer and
  date
- a format version, so later field renames don't break old entries

### 7. The page sits next to an existing "Activity" page

`/activity` and the dashboard's recent-activity widget already show
chronological feeds. Activity shows where each document stands now; the new
page shows what changed. The naming and placement must keep the two apart.

The page also needs:

- human labels instead of raw field names
- formatted money and dates
- names in place of ids where possible
- links to records that still exist
- filters for actor, entity type and a single record
- keyset pagination
- a way to collapse bulk system runs, for example "backfill updated 214
  documents"

### 8. Rollout and existing data

- **Deploy order.** Migrations run *after* the new container is live
  (`docs/deployment.md:99`). If the new code writes columns the migration has
  not added yet, every approve and amend fails until `kamal migrate` runs.
  - The change must ship in two releases: first create `audit_events`, then
    start writing to it. See Staging below.
- **No legacy rows.** `audit_events` starts empty on the day it ships.
  Nothing is copied from `event_logs`, so the page shows no history from
  before the release.
- **Timestamps** have one-second precision, so events from one transaction tie.
  Fix: `utc_datetime_usec`, order by `(inserted_at, id)`, and index
  `(user_id, inserted_at DESC, id DESC)`.
- **Tests that query `EventLog`** by `invoice_id` or `metadata` keys need
  updating: `accounting_test.exs`, `review_test.exs`.

### 9. Cost is not a concern

One user generates tens of audited changes a day: about 10k–30k rows a year,
a few MB with allowlisted diffs. Keeping entries forever costs almost nothing.
No pruning is needed.

## Goals vs. Non-Goals

* **In-Scope Goals:**
  * A read-only, newest-first audit page inside the existing
    `live_session :require_authenticated_user`. Reads filter by `%Scope{}`.
  * Every audited change writes its audit entry in the same transaction,
    including the two paths that are best-effort today.
  * Coverage:
    * changes to documents, review decisions, journal entries, postings,
      tax claims, financial accounts and balance snapshots, and the profile
      settings (display name, base currency)
    * one event per final extraction outcome, with the error class only
    * system and maintenance actions, each with a named actor
  * Field diffs limited to an allowlist per entity. Sensitive changes are
    recorded as "changed" with no value.
  * Entries readable after their subject is deleted.
  * Append-only, guarded against app bugs.
  * A serializable read function (`Audit.list_entries(scope, filters, cursor)`)
    that a later MCP endpoint can reuse.
  * Docs updated: `docs/architecture.md` §4, §5, §6.1, §8 (data model,
    security, tests), §9 (new decision), §10, §11, §12; `docs/operations.md`
    for any backfill or rollback steps.
* **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:**
  * Undo, retry, or any other action from the page.
  * The MCP endpoint and the authentication it would need.
  * Diagnostic detail: OCR text, LLM payloads, TypeSafe shadow results,
    per-attempt retry noise.
  * Deploy-time environment config.
  * Login and session tokens (unless decided otherwise).
  * Guarding against the operator. Append-only protects against app bugs, not
    someone with `psql`.
  * Retention, pruning, archiving.

## Alternatives Weighed

* **Carbonite (Postgres triggers with a transaction-metadata row).** It catches
  cascades, `update_all` and raw SQL, and is transactional by construction.
  Rejected as the default by the reviewers:
  * It records row changes, not domain events, so every table needs a
    translation layer before entries read like "Approved invoice X".
  * Every write path still has to insert a Carbonite transaction row first.
    That is the same wrapping work as explicit events.
  * It captures noise (`updated_at`-only changes, shadow writes) that has to be
    filtered out.
  * It captures every column by default, which works against the allowlist.
  * It remains the fallback if explicit events prove to leak.
* **ExAudit (Repo wrapper, actor in the process dictionary).** Rejected:
  * It doesn't see `update_all`, `insert_all`, `delete_all` or cascades.
  * Process-dictionary actors must be set again in every LiveView and Oban
    process.
  * It records row diffs, not domain events.
* **PaperTrail-style versioning.** Rejected. It gives the same guarantees as
  explicit events, plus a dependency and full-row snapshots by default.
* **A hand-written generic trigger (`to_jsonb(OLD)`/`to_jsonb(NEW)`).**
  Rejected. It captures every column, including fingerprints, account numbers
  and LLM payloads.
* **Explicit events plus a trigger-based catch-all table to check
  completeness.** Rejected as too heavy for a single-user app. It means two
  sources of truth.
* **Hash-chained, tamper-evident log.** Rejected. The operator could rebuild
  the chain, so it adds no real protection here.
* **Merged read model** (the page merges `audit_events` with existing
  `balance_snapshots` and `extracted_content` rows, like `Activity` does).
  Rejected by author: the existing rows have no actor column, so they can't
  say who made the change. Paging across several sources is awkward. One
  table costs only a few KB of duplicated data.
* **A Postgres view** (`UNION ALL` over the same tables). Rejected by author:
  it is the merged read model written in SQL. The source tables still have no
  actor, and every branch of the union needs its own index for keyset paging.
  A view could still be added later as a read layer over `audit_events`
  alone, for example for the MCP endpoint.
* **Reusing `event_logs`.** Rejected by author. Its `invoice_id` column holds
  ids from two different tables, its `status` column means nothing for an
  audit entry, and it has no actor. A new table avoids carrying those over.
  `event_logs` is frozen once `audit_events` covers the same events.
* **Nulling out the user on deletion (`on_delete: :nilify_all`).** Rejected:
  it works by updating audit rows, which the append-only trigger forbids.

## Key Decisions & Staging for Next Steps

**Converging recommendation from the reviewers.** All six agree on:

- explicit `Audit.record(...)` calls from each context, inside the same
  `Ecto.Multi` as the change
- one shared audit module, replacing the private `write_event_log` copies in
  `review.ex` and `accounting.ex`
- an actor passed explicitly, not through process state (decision 6 below
  carries it on `%Scope{}`)
- allowlisted field diffs in a `changes` jsonb column, with event context such
  as a rejection reason kept separate
- typed subjects with no foreign key, plus a label captured at write time
- `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` and `BEFORE TRUNCATE` triggers on the audit table
- coverage enforced by a test per public mutating function, and optionally a
  Credo check that flags `Repo.*` writes outside the audit helper

**Decided by the author (2026-11-04):**

1. **What one entry is.** One domain event per user or system operation.
   Each event holds a list of field diffs for the rows that operation changed.
2. **No extracted invoice fields in the trail.** Fields the LLM read from the
   document never appear in the log, as values or as diffs. These include
   issuer, invoice number, amount, date, currency and `reason_for_payment`,
   and the journal entry `description` copied from it. An amendment is
   recorded as an event that names the changed fields ("issuer, amount
   changed") with no values. User-entered fields can be diffed: category,
   need/want, notes, rejection reason, account names, balances and profile
   settings.
3. **New `audit_events` table. `event_logs` is frozen in a later release.** Its
   writers keep working until `audit_events` covers the same events, then they
   are removed. The table and its rows stay in place, unread, and none of its
   rows are copied. The author
   recalled `event_logs` as a possible event-sourcing experiment, but the
   written record says otherwise: spec `002-review-ocr-data`, the commit that
   added it (`1659de5`) and the `Review` moduledoc all describe it as the
   review audit trail, and no spec, doc or commit message mentions event
   sourcing. Session history does not reach back to when it was added. The
   docs must say that `audit_events` is the audit trail and that `event_logs`
   is a frozen, older review-only log (architecture §4, §5, §8 data model, and
   a new §9 decision that supersedes the audit part of D10).
4. **One table.** Every audited operation writes an `audit_events` row,
   including actions whose data already lives in insert-only tables (balance
   snapshots, extraction outcomes).
5. **Cascaded deletes and bulk updates are recorded explicitly.** A parent
   delete event lists what was deleted with it ("2 extractions, 1 review
   decision"; "5 balance snapshots"). `FingerprintBackfill` is rewritten to
   return the updated rows with their `user_id`. It then writes one summary
   event per run and one "fingerprint added" event per document, with no
   values. No database triggers capture changes.
6. **Actor carried on `%Scope{}`.** `Scope` gains an actor, for example
   `Scope.system(:recovery)` or `Scope.system(:fingerprint_backfill)`, and the
   writing functions in `Review` and `Accounting` move from a bare `user_id`
   to a `Scope`. OCR job args gain `initiated_by: upload | user_retry |
   recovery`, so the worker can rebuild the actor.
8. **Page name: "Audit log".** It is a separate page from Activity, inside
   `live_session :require_authenticated_user`.
9. **Success criteria (testable):**
   - every covered write path produces exactly one audit event, in the same
     transaction as the change
   - a test proves that no redacted field, extracted invoice field, or
     forbidden field reaches `audit_events`
   - a test with two users proves one user's events never appear for the other

7. **Deleting a user keeps their events.** `audit_events.user_id` (the owner)
   and the actor's user id are plain integer columns with no foreign key, so
   deleting a user neither fails nor touches audit rows. When the page or a
   later reader shows an actor whose user no longer exists, it shows a
   placeholder ("Deleted user"). Initials were rejected because they would
   have to be stored in each event, keeping part of the name after deletion.
   Record this in architecture §11. The frozen `event_logs.user_id` foreign
   key (`on_delete: :nothing`) still blocks deleting a user with old rows, so
   any future "delete user" feature needs a migration to drop that key.

**Staging:**

1. A refactor commit first: `Review` and `Accounting` writers take a `Scope`
   instead of `user_id`, and `Scope` gains an actor. No behaviour change.
2. Release N: create `audit_events` (append-only triggers, index on
   `(user_id, inserted_at DESC, id DESC)`). Because the table is new, the
   triggers can ship with it, and the previous release never touches it.
3. Release N+1: the shared `Audit` module and all writers. This release also
   adds `initiated_by` to the OCR job args and rewrites `FingerprintBackfill`.
   Old jobs without `initiated_by` default to `upload`.
4. Release N+1 or N+2: the "Audit log" page and its read function
   `Audit.list_entries(scope, filters, cursor)`.
5. Final release, once `audit_events` is confirmed to cover approve, amend,
   reject, post and file-reuse events: freeze `event_logs`. Remove its writers
   and the `EventLog` schema, and update the tests that query it
   (`accounting_test.exs`, `review_test.exs`). Leave the table and its rows in
   place.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Glob

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. 1	---
2	name: egm-comprehension
3	description: Naive Reader persona auditing documents with zero assumed institutional knowledge, flagging undefined terms, acronyms, and comprehension gaps.
4	license: Apache-2.0
5	---
6	
7	# Core Mandates (Universal Goldfish Context)
8	
9	You are a specialized Goldfish subagent operating within the Elephant-Goldfish Model. You have been delegated a specific task by the root agent (the Elephant).
10	
11	1. **Strict Read-Only Protocol**: You are a strictly read-only agent. You have NO tools to modify the workspace, write files, or compile code. Do not attempt to fix or refactor any code.
12	2. **Stateless Mindset (Goldfish Isolation)**: You evaluate plans with zero conversational history or external assumptions. You must read the document as a naive team member or fresh reader who has just joined the project.
13	3. **No Chitchat**: Avoid conversational filler. Focus exclusively on technical rationale and findings. Do not narrate your tool usage.
14	
15	---
16	
17	# Role
18	
19	You are **Comprehension Goldfish**.
20	You behave as a naive team member or a fresh reader who has just joined the project. You have no prior historical context or unstated project knowledge. You expect explanations to be clear, logical, and self-contained. You do not accept hand-waving or vague descriptions, and you flag any concept that is not either defined inline or linked to external documentation.
21	
22	---
23	
24	# Instructions
25	
26	Inspect the `Mode` parameter specified by the caller:
27	
28	### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM (Upstream Concept Ideation)
29	Evaluate the raw feature concept for UX, developer ergonomics, and cognitive overhead:
30	1. **API / CLI Ergonomics**: Is the proposed interface or workflow intuitive? Does it match standard developer conventions and established ecosystem practices?
31	2. **Cognitive Friction**: Are error messages actionable, or does the concept introduce unnecessary developer complexity?
32	3. Report UX and ergonomics feedback back to the orchestrator.
33	
34	### IF Mode: REVIEW (Document Audit)
35	Audit the target document file and line range specified by the caller:
36	
37	1. **Paraphrase First**: In your own words, write what the document proposes and how the existing system works, as the document describes it. If you cannot write a paraphrase of a section, report that section as a 🔴 Blocker. A list of undefined terms does not find a document whose terms are all defined but whose parts do not connect. The paraphrase does.
38	2. **Evaluate Clarity**: Read the active target scope to assess the flow and clarity of explanations.
39	3. **Verify Definitions & Links**: Identify any custom terms, services, systems, or architectural concepts referenced in the active scope. Verify that each is defined within the document (either inline, in an earlier section, or in a local glossary) or accompanied by a link to its documentation.
40	4. **Self-Containment Check**: If a term is not defined within the active target scope, scan the rest of the target document to see if it was defined elsewhere before flagging it as a gap.
41	5. **Check for Assumed Knowledge**: Audit the explanations to ensure they do not assume the reader knows unstated prerequisites, dependencies, or side-effects.
42	
43	### Audit Vectors:
44	* **Undefined or Unlinked Concepts**: Referencing components, tools, or systems without a brief definition or a link to their documentation.
45	* **Assumed Workflow Prerequisites**: Describing how to execute a task or workflow while assuming the reader already knows the unstated setup steps.
46	* **Vague Explanations**: Using imprecise descriptions (e.g., "the system handles this automatically" without explaining or linking to *how* it handles it).
47	
48	You do not know **this project**. You do know software. Flag a term only when it is specific to this project, team, or design and is not defined. Do not flag general engineering terms.
49	
50	---
51	
52	# Output Format
53	
54	Report your findings back to the orchestrator in plain, natural language.
55	
56	#### IF Mode: REVIEW
57	Start with your paraphrase, under two headings: **What this proposes** and **How the existing system works, per this document** (2-5 sentences each). The author compares it with the intent. A wrong paraphrase is a finding.
58	
59	Then, for each finding, include:
60	1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
61	2. **Affected Scope**: Section heading, concept term, or line numbers.
62	3. **Discrepancy Description & Rationale**: Explanation of the clarity gap or unstated assumption.
63	
64	#### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM
65	For each UX or ergonomics issue, include:
66	1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
67	2. **Dimension**: UX & Developer Ergonomics
68	3. **Usability Friction**: Non-intuitive API/CLI contract, vague error behavior, or high cognitive load.
69	4. **Ergonomic Requirement**: Mandatory UX/ergonomics standard for the Concepts Brief/PRD.
70

1	# User-visible audit trail
2	
3	* **Author:** Alexis Cramatte
4	* **Date:** 2026-11-03
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	ZaimuTomo gets a read-only page where the user can see what changed in their
9	data, when it changed, and who changed it: the user, or a named system process
10	such as document processing, startup recovery, or a maintenance task. The page
11	is for looking only. It has no undo and no retry. Later, an MCP endpoint could
12	expose the same log to agents.
13	
14	The app already writes an audit table, `event_logs`, but it is narrow:
15	
16	- It covers four review and posting events.
17	- Two of those four are written after the change commits, on a best-effort
18	  basis. If the insert fails, the row is lost and only a warning is logged:
19	  `Review.reject_invoice` (`lib/zaimu_tomo/review.ex:96`) and
20	  `Accounting.post_entry` (`lib/zaimu_tomo/accounting.ex:352`).
21	- Its `invoice_id` column holds an extraction id for review events and a
22	  journal-entry id for posting events, with nothing in the row to say which.
23	- No page shows it.
24	
25	This feature turns that table into a complete, user-readable history.
26	
27	## Analysis
28	
29	Six independent reviewers looked at the hypothesis. Their findings, merged and
30	sorted by theme:
31	
32	### 1. Completeness is the main risk, not storage or UI
33	
34	A history log that misses changes is worse than none, because the user will
35	trust its gaps. The reviewers listed every write path for the covered data. These
36	are the ones a simple "log it in the context function" approach would miss:
37	
38	- **Database cascades.** Deleting a document cascades through
39	  `extracted_content` to `review_decisions`. Deleting a financial account
40	  cascades to `balance_snapshots`. No Elixir code sees those child deletes.
41	- **`Repo.update_all` in `FingerprintBackfill`** (`fingerprint_backfill.ex:128`).
42	  It writes documents without going through a changeset and doesn't return the
43	  rows. The same task also changes journal entries (sets the reuse
44	  confirmation) and keeps `updated_at` unchanged on purpose.
45	- **Public writers that nothing in the app calls yet.** Any future caller would
46	  skip the audit:
47	  - `Accounting.create_from_decision/2`, which only tests use
48	  - `Review.update_review_decision/2`
49	  - `FinancialAccounts.update_financial_account/3` and `delete_financial_account/2`
50	- **Data migrations** that run raw `UPDATE` statements, for example
51	  `20260804100341_set_base_currency_default.exs`.
52	- **Dev seeds.** They would appear as user actions unless they get their own actor.
53	
54	No web or mix-task code calls `Repo` directly, so writing events from the
55	contexts reaches everything except the cascades, `update_all`, and migrations.
56	Those need explicit handling (see Key Decisions).
57	
58	### 2. Every audited write must commit together with its change
59	
60	Decision D10 in `docs/architecture.md` already requires this for approve and
61	amend. Rejection and posting do not follow it, and none of the new paths
62	(documents, accounts, balances, settings) have any audit write yet. The
63	reviewers agree the rule should extend to every audited change: if the audit
64	insert fails, the change rolls back. The case against: a bug in the audit
65	insert would block a save. For a permanent single-user ledger, a loud failure
66	is better than a silent gap, and tests can catch audit-insert bugs.
67	
68	### 3. "Before/after values" conflicts with "no document text"
69	
70	The issuer, invoice number, amount, date and `reason_for_payment` on review
71	decisions and journal entries are all LLM output from reading the document.
72	Read literally, "never store document text" forbids the diffs the page exists
73	to show. Existing `invoice_amended` rows already store the full
74	`amended_data`. Other fields must never appear at all:
75	
76	- fingerprints (`content_sha256`, `source_document_sha256`). Architecture §8
77	  says they are "never rendered", and the schemas mark them `redact: true`.
78	- `hashed_password`
79	- `raw_llm_response`, `analysis` and `error_details`
80	
81	The reviewers recommend:
82	
83	- **An allowlist of fields per entity, not a denylist.** With a denylist, every
84	  new column would leak into the log until someone excluded it.
85	- **Ecto's redacted fields** (`__schema__(:redact_fields)`) stripped as a
86	  backstop.
87	- **A clear boundary**, which the author has since set more strictly than the
88	  reviewers proposed (decision 2 below): extracted invoice fields are not
89	  recorded at all, only user-entered fields are.
90	
91	### 4. Most of the coverage list already has history
92	
93	Some covered items already keep their own history:
94	
95	- Extraction attempts are separate `extracted_content` rows, never edited.
96	- Balance snapshots are only ever inserted.
97	- Review decisions move forward once.
98	
99	Only about eight call sites overwrite or delete user data:
100	
101	- `post_entry` (re-categorizing, tax claim)
102	- account update and delete
103	- document update and delete
104	- profile update
105	- reject
106	- the fingerprint backfill
107	
108	Logging the insert-only data again duplicates facts. The other option is to
109	build the page as a read model, like `ZaimuTomo.Activity`, that merges
110	`event_logs` with those existing rows. The zoom-out reviewer prefers that.
111	Others prefer one table for one consistent "who" column and simpler paging.
112	The author chose one table (decision 4 below).
113	
114	### 5. "Who" needs an owner, an actor, and a way to carry it
115	
116	- **Two fields, not one.** A single `user_id` cannot hold both whose data it is
117	  and who did it.
118	- **Actors are lost across Oban.** Upload, user retry, Recovery, and a Lifeline
119	  rescue all end in the same `Worker` write. The job args carry no origin, so
120	  these four cases cannot be told apart.
121	- **Module names change.** Entries are kept forever, so the actor needs a
122	  stable key such as `system.ocr_job` or `release.fingerprint_backfill`, with a
123	  display label.
124	- **The actor has no carrier.** `Scope` holds only `user`. Review and
125	  Accounting take a bare `user_id`. Release tasks have neither.
126	
127	### 6. Entries must outlive the records they describe
128	
129	Documents and accounts can be hard-deleted. A foreign key from an audit row to
130	its subject would either block the delete or delete the history with it. Each
131	entry needs:
132	
133	- a typed subject (`subject_type` + `subject_id`) with no foreign key
134	- a short label captured at write time, for example a filename, or issuer and
135	  date
136	- a format version, so later field renames don't break old entries
137	
138	### 7. The page sits next to an existing "Activity" page
139	
140	`/activity` and the dashboard's recent-activity widget already show
141	chronological feeds. Activity shows where each document stands now; the new
142	page shows what changed. The naming and placement must keep the two apart.
143	
144	The page also needs:
145	
146	- human labels instead of raw field names
147	- formatted money and dates
148	- names in place of ids where possible
149	- links to records that still exist
150	- filters for actor, entity type and a single record
151	- keyset pagination
152	- a way to collapse bulk system runs, for example "backfill updated 214
153	  documents"
154	
155	### 8. Rollout and existing data
156	
157	- **Deploy order.** Migrations run *after* the new container is live
158	  (`docs/deployment.md:99`). If the new code writes columns the migration has
159	  not added yet, every approve and amend fails until `kamal migrate` runs.
160	  - The change must ship in two releases: first create `audit_events`, then
161	    start writing to it. See Staging below.
162	- **No legacy rows.** `audit_events` starts empty on the day it ships.
163	  Nothing is copied from `event_logs`, so the page shows no history from
164	  before the release.
165	- **Timestamps** have one-second precision, so events from one transaction tie.
166	  Fix: `utc_datetime_usec`, order by `(inserted_at, id)`, and index
167	  `(user_id, inserted_at DESC, id DESC)`.
168	- **Tests that query `EventLog`** by `invoice_id` or `metadata` keys need
169	  updating: `accounting_test.exs`, `review_test.exs`.
170	
171	### 9. Cost is not a concern
172	
173	One user generates tens of audited changes a day: about 10k–30k rows a year,
174	a few MB with allowlisted diffs. Keeping entries forever costs almost nothing.
175	No pruning is needed.
176	
177	## Goals vs. Non-Goals
178	
179	* **In-Scope Goals:**
180	  * A read-only, newest-first audit page inside the existing
181	    `live_session :require_authenticated_user`. Reads filter by `%Scope{}`.
182	  * Every audited change writes its audit entry in the same transaction,
183	    including the two paths that are best-effort today.
184	  * Coverage:
185	    * changes to documents, review decisions, journal entries, postings,
186	      tax claims, financial accounts and balance snapshots, and the profile
187	      settings (display name, base currency)
188	    * one event per final extraction outcome, with the error class only
189	    * system and maintenance actions, each with a named actor
190	  * Field diffs limited to an allowlist per entity. Sensitive changes are
191	    recorded as "changed" with no value.
192	  * Entries readable after their subject is deleted.
193	  * Append-only, guarded against app bugs.
194	  * A serializable read function (`Audit.list_entries(scope, filters, cursor)`)
195	    that a later MCP endpoint can reuse.
196	  * Docs updated: `docs/architecture.md` §4, §5, §6.1, §8 (data model,
197	    security, tests), §9 (new decision), §10, §11, §12; `docs/operations.md`
198	    for any backfill or rollback steps.
199	* **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:**
200	  * Undo, retry, or any other action from the page.
201	  * The MCP endpoint and the authentication it would need.
202	  * Diagnostic detail: OCR text, LLM payloads, TypeSafe shadow results,
203	    per-attempt retry noise.
204	  * Deploy-time environment config.
205	  * Login and session tokens (unless decided otherwise).
206	  * Guarding against the operator. Append-only protects against app bugs, not
207	    someone with `psql`.
208	  * Retention, pruning, archiving.
209	
210	## Alternatives Weighed
211	
212	* **Carbonite (Postgres triggers with a transaction-metadata row).** It catches
213	  cascades, `update_all` and raw SQL, and is transactional by construction.
214	  Rejected as the default by the reviewers:
215	  * It records row changes, not domain events, so every table needs a
216	    translation layer before entries read like "Approved invoice X".
217	  * Every write path still has to insert a Carbonite transaction row first.
218	    That is the same wrapping work as explicit events.
219	  * It captures noise (`updated_at`-only changes, shadow writes) that has to be
220	    filtered out.
221	  * It captures every column by default, which works against the allowlist.
222	  * It remains the fallback if explicit events prove to leak.
223	* **ExAudit (Repo wrapper, actor in the process dictionary).** Rejected:
224	  * It doesn't see `update_all`, `insert_all`, `delete_all` or cascades.
225	  * Process-dictionary actors must be set again in every LiveView and Oban
226	    process.
227	  * It records row diffs, not domain events.
228	* **PaperTrail-style versioning.** Rejected. It gives the same guarantees as
229	  explicit events, plus a dependency and full-row snapshots by default.
230	* **A hand-written generic trigger (`to_jsonb(OLD)`/`to_jsonb(NEW)`).**
231	  Rejected. It captures every column, including fingerprints, account numbers
232	  and LLM payloads.
233	* **Explicit events plus a trigger-based catch-all table to check
234	  completeness.** Rejected as too heavy for a single-user app. It means two
235	  sources of truth.
236	* **Hash-chained, tamper-evident log.** Rejected. The operator could rebuild
237	  the chain, so it adds no real protection here.
238	* **Merged read model** (the page merges `audit_events` with existing
239	  `balance_snapshots` and `extracted_content` rows, like `Activity` does).
240	  Rejected by author: the existing rows have no actor column, so they can't
241	  say who made the change. Paging across several sources is awkward. One
242	  table costs only a few KB of duplicated data.
243	* **A Postgres view** (`UNION ALL` over the same tables). Rejected by author:
244	  it is the merged read model written in SQL. The source tables still have no
245	  actor, and every branch of the union needs its own index for keyset paging.
246	  A view could still be added later as a read layer over `audit_events`
247	  alone, for example for the MCP endpoint.
248	* **Reusing `event_logs`.** Rejected by author. Its `invoice_id` column holds
249	  ids from two different tables, its `status` column means nothing for an
250	  audit entry, and it has no actor. A new table avoids carrying those over.
251	  `event_logs` is frozen once `audit_events` covers the same events.
252	* **Nulling out the user on deletion (`on_delete: :nilify_all`).** Rejected:
253	  it works by updating audit rows, which the append-only trigger forbids.
254	
255	## Key Decisions & Staging for Next Steps
256	
257	**Converging recommendation from the reviewers.** All six agree on:
258	
259	- explicit `Audit.record(...)` calls from each context, inside the same
260	  `Ecto.Multi` as the change
261	- one shared audit module, replacing the private `write_event_log` copies in
262	  `review.ex` and `accounting.ex`
263	- an actor passed explicitly, not through process state (decision 6 below
264	  carries it on `%Scope{}`)
265	- allowlisted field diffs in a `changes` jsonb column, with event context such
266	  as a rejection reason kept separate
267	- typed subjects with no foreign key, plus a label captured at write time
268	- `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` and `BEFORE TRUNCATE` triggers on the audit table
269	- coverage enforced by a test per public mutating function, and optionally a
270	  Credo check that flags `Repo.*` writes outside the audit helper
271	
272	**Decided by the author (2026-11-04):**
273	
274	1. **What one entry is.** One domain event per user or system operation.
275	   Each event holds a list of field diffs for the rows that operation changed.
276	2. **No extracted invoice fields in the trail.** Fields the LLM read from the
277	   document never appear in the log, as values or as diffs. These include
278	   issuer, invoice number, amount, date, currency and `reason_for_payment`,
279	   and the journal entry `description` copied from it. An amendment is
280	   recorded as an event that names the changed fields ("issuer, amount
281	   changed") with no values. User-entered fields can be diffed: category,
282	   need/want, notes, rejection reason, account names, balances and profile
283	   settings.
284	3. **New `audit_events` table. `event_logs` is frozen in a later release.** Its
285	   writers keep working until `audit_events` covers the same events, then they
286	   are removed. The table and its rows stay in place, unread, and none of its
287	   rows are copied. The author
288	   recalled `event_logs` as a possible event-sourcing experiment, but the
289	   written record says otherwise: spec `002-review-ocr-data`, the commit that
290	   added it (`1659de5`) and the `Review` moduledoc all describe it as the
291	   review audit trail, and no spec, doc or commit message mentions event
292	   sourcing. Session history does not reach back to when it was added. The
293	   docs must say that `audit_events` is the audit trail and that `event_logs`
294	   is a frozen, older review-only log (architecture §4, §5, §8 data model, and
295	   a new §9 decision that supersedes the audit part of D10).
296	4. **One table.** Every audited operation writes an `audit_events` row,
297	   including actions whose data already lives in insert-only tables (balance
298	   snapshots, extraction outcomes).
299	5. **Cascaded deletes and bulk updates are recorded explicitly.** A parent
300	   delete event lists what was deleted with it ("2 extractions, 1 review
301	   decision"; "5 balance snapshots"). `FingerprintBackfill` is rewritten to
302	   return the updated rows with their `user_id`. It then writes one summary
303	   event per run and one "fingerprint added" event per document, with no
304	   values. No database triggers capture changes.
305	6. **Actor carried on `%Scope{}`.** `Scope` gains an actor, for example
306	   `Scope.system(:recovery)` or `Scope.system(:fingerprint_backfill)`, and the
307	   writing functions in `Review` and `Accounting` move from a bare `user_id`
308	   to a `Scope`. OCR job args gain `initiated_by: upload | user_retry |
309	   recovery`, so the worker can rebuild the actor.
310	8. **Page name: "Audit log".** It is a separate page from Activity, inside
311	   `live_session :require_authenticated_user`.
312	9. **Success criteria (testable):**
313	   - every covered write path produces exactly one audit event, in the same
314	     transaction as the change
315	   - a test proves that no redacted field, extracted invoice field, or
316	     forbidden field reaches `audit_events`
317	   - a test with two users proves one user's events never appear for the other
318	
319	7. **Deleting a user keeps their events.** `audit_events.user_id` (the owner)
320	   and the actor's user id are plain integer columns with no foreign key, so
321	   deleting a user neither fails nor touches audit rows. When the page or a
322	   later reader shows an actor whose user no longer exists, it shows a
323	   placeholder ("Deleted user"). Initials were rejected because they would
324	   have to be stored in each event, keeping part of the name after deletion.
325	   Record this in architecture §11. The frozen `event_logs.user_id` foreign
326	   key (`on_delete: :nothing`) still blocks deleting a user with old rows, so
327	   any future "delete user" feature needs a migration to drop that key.
328	
329	**Staging:**
330	
331	1. A refactor commit first: `Review` and `Accounting` writers take a `Scope`
332	   instead of `user_id`, and `Scope` gains an actor. No behaviour change.
333	2. Release N: create `audit_events` (append-only triggers, index on
334	   `(user_id, inserted_at DESC, id DESC)`). Because the table is new, the
335	   triggers can ship with it, and the previous release never touches it.
336	3. Release N+1: the shared `Audit` module and all writers. This release also
337	   adds `initiated_by` to the OCR job args and rewrites `FingerprintBackfill`.
338	   Old jobs without `initiated_by` default to `upload`.
339	4. Release N+1 or N+2: the "Audit log" page and its read function
340	   `Audit.list_entries(scope, filters, cursor)`.
341	5. Final release, once `audit_events` is confirmed to cover approve, amend,
342	   reject, post and file-reuse events: freeze `event_logs`. Remove its writers
343	   and the `EventLog` schema, and update the tests that query it
344	   (`accounting_test.exs`, `review_test.exs`). Leave the table and its rows in
345	   place.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## funes
Persistent memory over the user's past AI coding sessions: their transcripts, indexed automatically as they work and read-only here — nothing has to be saved. When earlier work matters, this is the memory to consult.
I have the brief and persona. Next I'm checking the brief's factual anchors against the codebase, since a fresh reader would rely on them.

Notes:

- Kamal performs a zero-downtime switch at the proxy. In-flight Oban jobs on the old container are rescued by `Oban.Lifeline` after 30 minutes, if they don't finish during shutdown.
- Migrations run *after* the new container is live, so write migrations that the previous release can run against (additive first, destructive later).
- Kamal aliases (`config/deploy.yml` → `aliases`) are invoked directly: `kamal console`, `kamal migrate`, `kamal db_rollback`, `kamal verify_storage`, `kamal recover_stuck_documents`, `kamal backfill_document_fingerprints`, `kamal migrate_to_s3`.

## CI

GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs on pushes to `main` and on every
PR, for any base branch so stacked PRs are covered, as three jobs: `lint` (format
check, blocking `mix credo --strict`, unused-dependency check), `test` (compiles
with warnings as errors, migrates a Postgres 18 service, runs `mix test`), and `security-audit`
(`mix hex.audit`, advisory/non-blocking — a new CVE in an unrelated dependency
shouldn't block unrelated work). A separate scheduled workflow
